overview: The Anambé are an Indigenous people of Pará in northern Brazil, with a community on the Cairari River in the Moju basin. Their language belongs to the Tupi-Guarani family. Histories of movement and severe disruption coexist with continuing family life, farming, craft knowledge and cultural renewal.

periods.title: Documenting a living community
periods.summary: Researchers visited the Cairari community and formed ethnographic collections in 1969. Later work reconnected community memories with these objects, challenging earlier outside assumptions that the Anambé had disappeared.

periods.title: Transfer and return
periods.summary: Anambé families were transferred to Alto Rio Guamá and returned to the Cairari region during 1982. Their movement helps explain why later population counts differ and why a single village count cannot describe the whole people.

periods.title: Recognition of the Indigenous territory
periods.summary: Decree 380 recognized the administrative demarcation of the Anambé Indigenous area in Moju. Signed on December 24, it entered into force on publication on December 26, 1991, recognizing traditional occupation rather than creating a new people.

periods.title: A maker records her life and work
periods.summary: Luakam Anambé described her doll-making enterprise, family collaboration and hopes for learning the Anambé language. Her recorded testimony connects life in Rio de Janeiro with relationships to her people in Pará.

periods.title: A study of learning through play
periods.summary: An ethnographic study described children’s games and toys alongside elders’ memories. The authors explored how knowledge passes through making, watching, listening and playing in everyday places as well as through school.

items.text: ISA’s account describes gardens producing maize, rice and manioc flour, with surplus sold locally or to river traders. Hunting, fishing and gathering also supported households. These descriptions concern a changing twentieth-century economy, not a fixed diet shared by every family throughout Anambé history.

The same account records locally made carrying baskets, fans, sieves, spindles, mortars, boats and bows alongside purchased equipment. Useful skills persisted while materials and tools changed. Buying manufactured goods did not erase community identity or make the locally produced objects merely decorative.

The 1969 Cairari collection includes objects gathered from daily use and others made when researchers asked about less-used forms. Lisboa’s study distinguishes these circumstances. A museum collection can reveal skilled techniques without being a statistical sample of everything households used equally often.

Anambé baskets served different tasks: containers stored belongings, carrying baskets moved manioc, the jamaxim helped transport game, and a patrona held shotgun cartridges. Makers used fibers including timboí and arumã. Form and material therefore connect weaving knowledge with food production, transport and changing hunting equipment.

Lisboa brought photographs of collection objects to the village. Dona Tapira recalled gathering vines with her parents and recognized equipment associated with relatives. These conversations connected material descriptions with named people and lived experience. The encounter used photographs; it was not a physical return of the collection.

In the study published in 2022, elders remembered dolls made from parts of palm fruit clusters, miriti toy cars and small clay dishes. These were recalled childhood objects, not excavated artifacts. Turning familiar plants and earth into toys required knowledge of materials as well as imagination.

The researchers also observed children using handmade miniature bows, softwood or miriti boats, and clay dishes alongside shop-bought toys. They interpreted making models as practice in skills relevant to later work. The observations do not prove that every child followed the same learning path.

Children explained pisei, a game played on a ground drawing divided into squares. Players moved with closed eyes while asking a companion whether they had crossed a line. The account records rules, cooperation and attention to space, showing learning occurring through play outside a formal lesson.

Luakam Anambé’s 2021 interview describes the largely handmade Anaty dolls. She and her daughter made the clothing, while other workers helped with filling, hair and coloring. Her account makes visible the division of labor behind a finished object and connects craft income with family collaboration.

Luakam also spoke about an Indigenous language teacher in the community and her own plans to take lessons. She described receiving words from the teacher while living away from Pará. The testimony shows language renewal as deliberate learning and sustained relationships, rather than assuming that every Anambé person is already fluent.

Funai’s profile follows Luakam from sewing clothes by hand to factory work, buying a sewing machine and building a doll business. It also describes her Mãos de fadas project to help women acquire a trade. This is one maker’s documented achievement, not a timeless craft attributed to every Anambé household.

The 1991 decree identifies the Anambé area as traditionally and permanently occupied Indigenous land. Its boundary description uses rivers, streams and survey markers. This legal document is evidence for recognition of a specific territory; it does not verify this map’s much broader historical polygon or represent an ethnic founding date.

ending.text: Anambé people continue in the Cairari community and elsewhere. Migration, family ties, craft work and language learning are parts of that living history. Luakam’s account shows continuing relationships across distance. The imported map’s 1500 endpoint must not be read as the disappearance of the people.
